prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map places the tabletop, bowls, cups and candle within roughly 0.3–1.2 m of the camera wearer, while the seated people are approximately 1–2 m away across or beside the table; the room walls, doorway and cabinets are farther behind them, roughly 2–4 m away. Across the five frames, the nearest surface remains the table along the lower foreground, while the visible people shift from the left/front and right/front toward the right side as the camera turns; their changing image positions appear mainly due to camera rotation rather than clear approach or retreat. It clarifies foreground–background ordering and shows that tableware is within the camera wearer’s arm’s reach, with some bowls and cups also within reach of the people opposite, even where low light and motion blur obscure this in RGB. Depth around people’s limbs, the candle, reflective tableware, frame boundaries and the partly visible foreground person is smeared or merged, so metre estimates and person-to-object separations are approximate.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map identifies people, the dining table, bowls, cups and a refrigerator, separating overlapping objects that are difficult to distinguish in the dim, blurred RGB frames. In the first two frames, one person is partly cut off on the left and another is across the table toward the upper-right, with bowls and a cup between the camera wearer and the farther person; in the fourth and fifth frames, a person occupies the right/front side while the refrigerator remains behind and left of that person. The masks support relative placement but not metric distance: using the RGB and object scale, tabletop items are about 0.3–1.2 m from the camera wearer, people about 1–2 m away, and the refrigerator roughly 2–3 m away; bowls and cups near each person are generally within that person’s arm’s reach. The map is unreliable where masks disappear between frames, people or table regions merge, small labels overlap, and hands, arms, chairs and several pieces of tableware are omitted or only partially segmented, so facing direction and gaze cannot be determined confidently from it.
descriptions.pose: The pose map exposes articulated body and hand locations against the cluttered scene: little or no pose is recovered in the first three frames, while the fourth shows a yellow upper-body skeleton near the lower centre-right and magenta hand detections above/right, and the fifth shows a larger yellow skeleton on the right with a hand near the upper-right edge. In the later frames, the detected person is roughly 1–2 m from the camera wearer, facing mostly leftward or obliquely toward the table rather than clearly head-on; head and eye landmarks are too incomplete to establish whether the person looks at the camera wearer. The person’s arms extend toward the table, putting nearby bowls, cups and the table edge within roughly an arm’s reach, while some hands and limbs are partly outside the frame or occluded by the table and objects. The map makes limb orientation and the camera’s turn toward the right-side person easier to perceive than in RGB, but missing joints, detached hand traces, distorted skeleton geometry and absent detections in earlier frames make precise pose, gaze, distance and approach-versus-retreat judgments unreliable.
